name: Donepezil

lead: Donepezil is a prescription medicine for Alzheimer's dementia that increases acetylcholine in the brain. Some forum members ask about it as a nootropic.
Trials in dementia show modest cognitive benefits; its link to appearance is indirect, via cognitive performance.

paras: It reversibly blocks acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine lasts longer at synapses.
Nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, cramps and weight loss are common; the label warns of slow heart rate, heart block and GI bleeding. Prescription only.

forums.title: Where can I get Donepezil for my brain?

chain: Higher cholinergic signalling in the brain
Claimed sharper memory and focus for study, work and routine
angle.text: Some forum members discuss donepezil as a memory and focus aid. Its role in appearance is indirect, through whatever cognitive performance supports the rest of someone's looksmaxxing routine, such as planning, consistency and learning.

lead: Donepezil is a prescription cholinesterase inhibitor approved for dementia of the Alzheimer's type. By raising acetylcholine levels in the brain it is used to support memory and thinking. In looksmaxxing forums it comes up as a nootropic that some members ask about for focus and mental performance, an indirect route to ascending through better study, work and training consistency.[1][2][3]

It reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine. The US label states there is no evidence it alters the course of the underlying dementia.[1] Trials and reviews report modest cognitive benefits in Alzheimer's disease, and it has also been studied in Lewy body dementia, vascular dementia, mild cognitive impairment and other conditions.[4][5][6][7]

Donepezil was developed at the Japanese company Eisai, where research on the compound began in 1983 under Hachiro Sugimoto, and the FDA approved it in 1996 under the brand name Aricept.[7][8] It later became the world's best-selling Alzheimer's treatment and is now available as a generic.[7]

Common adverse reactions are nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, vomiting, muscle cramps, fatigue and anorexia, and the label warns of slowed heart rate and heart block, among other precautions.[3] It is available by prescription; one looksmax.org thread title shows members asking where to obtain it.[9]
infobox: Oral tablet, orally disintegrating tablet, transdermal patch

paras: The labelled use is symptomatic treatment of dementia of the Alzheimer's type at mild, moderate and severe stages.[3] Wikipedia states that it gives a small benefit in mental function and daily functioning without slowing disease progression, and that treatment should stop if no benefit is seen.[7] NICE in the UK recommends it for mild to moderate disease with frequent review.[7]

Clinicians also prescribe it off-label for conditions such as dementia with Lewy bodies.[5][1] Wikipedia lists further investigational uses, including vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease dementia, traumatic brain injury, and exploratory work in autism, ADHD, Tourette syndrome, sleep apnea, anorexia nervosa and multiple sclerosis-related cognitive impairment, with mixed or limited results.[7] Registered trials have included Alzheimer's, Lewy body dementia, cerebrovascular dementia and autism populations.[10][11]
In the United States it was reported as the 126th most commonly prescribed medication in 2023, with more than four million prescriptions.[7]

Donepezil is rarely discussed on looksmaxxing forums. Where it appears, it is in nootropic-style questions from members who want a cognitive edge and ask how to obtain it, framed around memory and mental performance rather than any direct change in looks.[9] The connection to appearance runs through cognition: better learning, planning and consistency could support the study, work and training habits that other looksmaxxing practices depend on. Its place in the wiki is as a drug people ask about, not a recognised appearance treatment.

Research at Eisai began in 1983, led by Hachiro Sugimoto at the company's Tsukuba Research Laboratories, where the compound was known by the code E2020.[7][8] Wikipedia's biography of Sugimoto, born in Tokyo in 1943, says his mother's dementia was a personal motivation and that the work was guided by the hypothesis linking acetylcholine to memory decline.[8] His later awards included the 1998 Special Galien Prize and the 2002 Imperial Award for Invention.[8]

The cholinergic hypothesis, reviewed in a widely cited 1999 paper, attributes part of Alzheimer's memory loss to reduced cholinergic transmission and was the rationale for the drug class.[12] Donepezil was a second-generation cholinesterase inhibitor and the FDA approved it in 1996, co-marketed by Eisai and Pfizer.[7]

A 24-week placebo-controlled trial of donepezil in mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease was published in 1998 by the Donepezil Study Group. It randomised 473 patients to placebo or two donepezil dose arms; cognition on the ADAS-cog and clinician global ratings improved in both donepezil groups versus placebo, and scores were no longer different from placebo after a six-week washout.[13]

A 2012 trial of 295 community-dwelling patients with moderate to severe disease who had already taken donepezil examined continuing donepezil and adding memantine,[14] and a 2004 JAMA trial tested memantine added to ongoing donepezil.[15] A 2006 Cochrane review covered cholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer's disease as a class.[16]

In mild cognitive impairment, a three-year trial compared donepezil, vitamin E and placebo; Wikipedia's summary reports donepezil delayed progression to Alzheimer's diagnosis for roughly the first 18 months but not at 36 months, with a sustained effect in an APOE4 subgroup, and notes it is not indicated for dementia prevention.[17][7]

A 2024 meta-analysis found improved cognition across Alzheimer's drugs including cholinesterase inhibitors,[2] while a 2021 review described the benefit of the class as mild.[4] A 2015 meta-analysis reported benefits of donepezil and rivastigmine for cognitive and psychiatric symptoms in Lewy body dementia.[5]

Researchers have also studied donepezil in healthy volunteers' attention[18] and in cognitive impairment after breast cancer chemotherapy, in a 2024 phase III trial.[19] Wikipedia notes healthy-volunteer memory studies with mixed results: one 2009 study of 24 people reported improved spatial memory accuracy, while a 2011 study in older healthy adults reported impaired memory after acute and chronic dosing.[7]

The label lists nausea, diarrhea, insomnia, vomiting, muscle cramps, fatigue and anorexia as most common, and warns about bradycardia, heart block, GI bleeding risk and exaggerated succinylcholine muscle relaxation during anesthesia.[3] Wikipedia adds that nausea, diarrhea and vomiting are the main reasons for discontinuation, that vivid dreams or nightmares are reported, and that effects are usually mild and transient; seizures, abnormal heart rhythms and urinary incontinence are listed as more serious.[7] Caution is described for people with heart conduction disorders, asthma, COPD, peptic ulcer disease or NSAID use.[7]
Pregnancy data in humans are inadequate; animal studies did not show developmental toxicity during organogenesis.[3]

Donepezil reversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine at synapses.[3] The cholinergic hypothesis attributes part of Alzheimer's memory loss to reduced cholinergic transmission.[12][7] Donepezil is also described as a sigma-1 receptor agonist, which may contribute to anti-amnesic effects seen in animals.[7]

Reported pharmacokinetics are near-complete oral bioavailability, about 96 percent protein binding, peak levels at three to four hours, an elimination half-life of about 70 hours (longer in older adults) and metabolism by CYP2D6, CYP3A4 and glucuronidation.[1][7] It is marketed as a racemate.[7] A review of the class covers pharmacology and toxicology of cholinesterase inhibitors more broadly.[20]

Eisai began the research in 1983, led by Hachiro Sugimoto.[7][8] The FDA first approved donepezil in 1996, and approval was extended to severe Alzheimer's disease in 2006; a transdermal patch followed in 2022.[1][7] The first US generic, a Ranbaxy Labs formulation, became available in November 2010, and Aricept was reported as the world's best-selling Alzheimer's treatment in 2011.[7]
Donepezil is prescription-only in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada and Australia (Schedule 4), and is classified as a controlled substance in Brazil.[7]

Other cognitive-support supplements and drugs appear in the same nootropic discussions as donepezil. Choline alfoscerate, a cholinergic precursor, has been studied in a 2023 systematic review of adult-onset cognitive dysfunction and in a 2024 trial combining it with donepezil.[21][22] Memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, is the other major Alzheimer's drug class and is often studied alongside donepezil.[14][15]
